questions.stem: In physics, a field is best described as:
options: a region in which an object experiences a non-contact force
a region in which objects interact only when they are touching
the path a charged particle follows through a region of space
a region in which only charged particles can experience a force
questions.explanation: A field model explains forces between objects that are not in contact: a mass, charge or magnet sets up a field, and another object placed in that field experiences a force. Gravitational fields act on masses, so fields are not limited to charged particles.

questions.stem: What is the direction of the gravitational field around an isolated point mass?
options: Radially outward, away from the mass
questions.explanation: Gravitational field lines show the direction of the force on a test mass, and masses only attract, so the lines point radially inward. The field of a point mass is radial and non-uniform; it only looks uniform over a small region near a planet’s surface.

questions.stem: The direction of an electric field at a point is defined as the direction of the force on:
options: a small test mass placed at that point
the north pole of a small compass at that point
a small positive test charge placed at that point
a small negative test charge placed at that point
questions.explanation: By convention, electric field lines show the direction of the force on a positive test charge, so they point away from positive charges and towards negative ones. A negative charge experiences a force opposite to the field direction.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares monopoles and dipoles in the three fields?
options: Electric fields come only from dipoles, because positive and negative charges must pair
Electric fields can come from monopoles or dipoles, but no magnetic monopole has been observed
Gravitational fields come from dipoles, because every mass has two opposite poles
Magnetic monopoles are made by cutting a bar magnet so that each half has one pole
questions.explanation: A single charge is an electric monopole, and a pair of opposite charges is a dipole. Masses act as monopoles, as there is only one kind of mass. Cutting a bar magnet just makes two smaller magnets, each with a north and a south pole, so magnetic fields always come from dipoles.

questions.stem: Which of these pairs can only ever attract each other, never repel?
questions.explanation: Gravity is always attractive because there is only one kind of mass. Charges, magnetic poles and current-carrying conductors can attract or repel, depending on the signs of the charges, the poles involved or the directions of the currents.

questions.stem: Two long, straight, parallel wires carry currents in the same direction. What happens?
options: The wires twist to become perpendicular
The wires attract only if the currents are equal
questions.explanation: Each wire sits in the magnetic field of the other, and the force on a current in that field pulls the wires together when the currents are in the same direction. Currents in opposite directions repel. The size of each current affects the size of the force, not whether it attracts.

questions.stem: Gravitational field strength at Earth’s surface is 9.8 N kg⁻¹. What is it at a height above the surface equal to Earth’s radius?
questions.explanation: The distance from Earth’s centre doubles, from R to 2R, and g follows an inverse square law, so it falls to a quarter: 9.8/4 ≈ 2.5 N kg⁻¹. Halving it treats the field as inversely proportional to distance, and 1.1 N kg⁻¹ mistakes the height for the distance from the centre and uses 3R.

questions.stem: What is the strength of the electric field 0.30 m from a 2.0 µC point charge? Use k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻².
questions.explanation: E = kq/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.30² ≈ 2.0 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹. Forgetting to square the distance gives 6.0 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹, and leaving the charge in coulombs without the micro prefix gives 2.0 × 10¹¹ N C⁻¹.

questions.stem: Two point charges repel with a force F. One charge is doubled and their separation is also doubled. What is the new force?
questions.explanation: Coulomb’s law gives F ∝ q₁q₂/r². Doubling one charge doubles the force, and doubling the separation divides it by 2² = 4, so the new force is 2F/4 = F/2. Treating the force as inversely proportional to r rather than r² gives F.

questions.stem: An electron is moved closer to a fixed negative point charge. What happens to the electric potential energy of the system?
options: It stays constant, because the field around the charge is radial
It increases, because work is done against the repulsion
It decreases, because the electron moves closer to the charge
It decreases, because the field does work on the electron
questions.explanation: Like charges repel, so pushing the electron closer requires work against the electric force, and that work is stored as potential energy. Potential energy decreases with approach only for attraction, such as a mass falling towards Earth or opposite charges coming together.

questions.stem: A space probe coasts directly away from Earth with its engines off. How do its gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy change?
options: Its potential energy increases and its kinetic energy decreases
Its potential energy decreases and its kinetic energy increases
Its potential energy and kinetic energy both decrease together
Its potential energy increases and its kinetic energy is constant
questions.explanation: Moving away from Earth is moving against the gravitational field, so gravitational potential energy rises. With no other forces doing work, that energy comes from the kinetic energy, so the probe slows down. The total of the two stays constant.

questions.stem: Outside a bar magnet, in which direction do the magnetic field lines run?
options: In straight lines parallel to the magnet
In circles around the magnet’s long axis
From the north pole to the south pole
From the south pole to the north pole
questions.explanation: By convention, field lines show the direction a compass north pole would point, so outside a magnet they leave the north pole and enter the south pole. Inside the magnet they run from south to north, completing closed loops.

questions.stem: A long straight wire passes vertically through a horizontal card and carries a current upward. Viewed from above, what do the magnetic field lines on the card look like?
options: Straight lines radiating out from the wire
Straight lines running parallel to each other
Anticlockwise circles centred on the wire
Clockwise circles centred on the wire
questions.explanation: By the right-hand grip rule, point the thumb along the current (upward, towards the viewer) and the fingers curl anticlockwise as seen from above. The field of a straight wire forms concentric circles, not radial lines, and reversing the current would make them clockwise.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the magnetic field inside a long, current-carrying solenoid?
options: It forms circles around the axis, like a straight wire
It is close to uniform and runs parallel to the axis
It is strongest near the wires and zero on the axis
It is radial, pointing outward from the central axis
questions.explanation: The fields of the many turns add inside a long solenoid to give a strong, nearly uniform field along its axis, much like a bar magnet. Outside, the field spreads out and is weaker.

questions.stem: You look at one end of a solenoid and see the conventional current flowing anticlockwise around it. That end of the solenoid behaves as:
options: a north pole only while the current is rising
neither pole, because its field is inside
questions.explanation: Curl the fingers of the right hand in the direction of the current and the thumb points to the north pole. Anticlockwise as you look at it puts the thumb towards you, so the end facing you is a north pole. A steady current gives a steady pole; it does not need to be changing.

questions.stem: The electric field between two large parallel plates connected to a steady DC supply, away from the edges, is best described as:
questions.explanation: A steady supply gives a field that does not change with time, so it is static. Between large parallel plates, away from the edges, the field has the same strength and direction everywhere, so it is uniform. The field of a point charge, by contrast, is non-uniform.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a changing field?
options: The magnetic field of a coil carrying a 50 Hz AC current
The electric field between plates on a steady DC supply
The magnetic field of a bar magnet at rest on a bench
Earth’s gravitational field at a point near its surface
questions.explanation: An alternating current reverses fifty times a second, so the magnetic field it produces changes continuously. The other fields are static: they do not vary with time, even though some of them, such as the bar magnet’s, are non-uniform in space.

questions.stem: Two parallel plates 5.0 mm apart have a potential difference of 200 V across them. What is the electric field strength between them?
questions.explanation: For a uniform field, E = V/d = 200/(5.0 × 10⁻³) = 4.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹. Using 5 instead of 5.0 × 10⁻³ m gives 40 V m⁻¹, and multiplying V by d gives 1.0 × 10³.

questions.stem: An electron is in a uniform electric field of strength 2.5 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. What is the size of the electric force on it? Use e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
questions.explanation: F = qE = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.5 × 10⁴ = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ N. Dividing the charge by the field gives 6.4 × 10⁻²⁴ N. The force on an electron acts opposite to the field direction, towards the positive plate.

questions.stem: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 500 V. What is its final speed? Use e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and electron mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
questions.explanation: The work done is W = qV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 500 = 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷ J, which becomes kinetic energy: v = √(2 × 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁷/9.1 × 10⁻³¹) ≈ 1.3 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹. Leaving out the 2 gives 9.4 × 10⁶, and forgetting the square root gives 1.8 × 10¹⁴, which is v².

questions.stem: An alpha particle, with charge +2e, is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 1000 V. How much kinetic energy does it gain?
questions.explanation: The energy gained is W = qV. With q = 2e and V = 1000 V, W = 2000 eV, since one electron-volt is the energy one elementary charge gains through 1 V. Using a single charge gives 1000 eV.

questions.stem: An electron moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a uniform 0.050 T magnetic field. What is the size of the magnetic force on it? Use e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
questions.explanation: F = qvB = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁶ × 0.050 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. Leaving out the field gives 3.2 × 10⁻¹³ N, and dividing by B instead of multiplying gives 6.4 × 10⁻¹² N.

questions.stem: An electron moves parallel to a uniform magnetic field. What is the magnetic force on it?
options: Zero, so its path is unchanged
qvB, at right angles to its path
questions.explanation: The magnetic force on a moving charge depends on the component of velocity perpendicular to the field. Moving parallel to the field, that component is zero, so there is no force and the electron continues in a straight line.

questions.stem: An electron travels north into a uniform magnetic field directed vertically downward. In which direction is the magnetic force on the electron as it enters the field?
questions.explanation: For a positive charge moving north in a downward field, the right-hand rule gives a force to the west. An electron is negative, so its force is reversed, to the east. Forgetting to reverse for the negative charge is the usual slip here.

questions.stem: An electron moves at 3.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a uniform 2.0 × 10⁻³ T magnetic field. What is the radius of its circular path? Use e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and electron mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
questions.explanation: r = mv/(qB) = (9.1 × 10⁻³¹ × 3.0 × 10⁶)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁻³) ≈ 8.5 × 10⁻³ m. Using the proton mass gives about 16 m, and inverting the fraction gives 1.2 × 10² m.

questions.stem: In a uniform magnetic field, an electron’s speed is doubled and the field strength is halved. How does the radius of its circular path change?
options: It becomes a quarter as large
It becomes four times as large
questions.explanation: Since r = mv/(qB), the radius is proportional to v and inversely proportional to B. Doubling v doubles r, and halving B doubles it again, so r becomes four times as large. Thinking the two changes cancel gives ‘the same’.

questions.stem: Why does a uniform magnetic field not change the speed of an electron moving perpendicular to it?
options: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work
The force acts along the velocity, so it changes only the direction
The force acts only at the moment the electron enters the field
The force is balanced by the electron’s weight, so the net force is zero
questions.explanation: The magnetic force is always at right angles to the velocity, so it has no component along the motion and does no work. It changes the direction of the velocity but not its size, which produces uniform circular motion. A force along the velocity would change the speed.

questions.stem: Outside a planet, how does the planet’s gravitational field strength depend on the distance r from its centre?
options: It is directly proportional to r²
It is the same at every distance r
It is inversely proportional to r²
It is inversely proportional to r
questions.explanation: g = GM/r², so the field obeys an inverse square law: doubling the distance from the centre reduces the field to a quarter. It only seems constant near the surface, where r changes very little.

questions.stem: Mars has a mass of 6.4 × 10²³ kg and a radius of 3.4 × 10⁶ m. What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
questions.explanation: g = GM/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.4 × 10²³ / (3.4 × 10⁶)² ≈ 3.7 N kg⁻¹. Forgetting to square the radius gives 1.3 × 10⁷ N kg⁻¹. The value 9.8 N kg⁻¹ applies only at Earth’s surface.

questions.stem: What is the gravitational force on a 70 kg astronaut aboard a space station 6.8 × 10⁶ m from Earth’s centre? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and Earth’s mass 5.98 × 10²⁴ kg.
questions.explanation: F = GMm/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.98 × 10²⁴ × 70 / (6.8 × 10⁶)² ≈ 6.0 × 10² N, still most of the astronaut’s surface weight of 6.9 × 10² N. The force is far from zero: it is what keeps the astronaut in orbit.

questions.stem: The area under a graph of Earth’s gravitational field strength against distance from its centre, between 7.0 × 10⁶ m and 8.0 × 10⁶ m, is 7.1 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. How much energy is needed to lift a 500 kg satellite between these distances?
questions.explanation: The area under a field–distance graph is the change in potential energy per kilogram, so multiply by the mass: 7.1 × 10⁶ × 500 ≈ 3.6 × 10⁹ J. 7.1 × 10⁶ J leaves out the mass, and 3.5 × 10¹⁰ J multiplies by g as well, which the area already accounts for.

questions.stem: The area under a graph of the gravitational force on a rocket against its distance from Earth’s centre, between two distances, gives:
options: the change in the rocket’s momentum between those points
the gravitational field strength between those points
the impulse that gravity gives to the rocket between them
the change in the rocket’s gravitational potential energy
questions.explanation: Force multiplied by distance is work, so the area under a force–distance graph is the work done against gravity, which equals the change in gravitational potential energy. Impulse and change in momentum come from the area under a force–time graph.

questions.stem: A satellite orbits at 4.2 × 10⁷ m from Earth’s centre. Modelled as uniform circular motion, what is its orbital speed? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and Earth’s mass 5.98 × 10²⁴ kg.
questions.explanation: Gravity provides the centripetal force, GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.98 × 10²⁴ / 4.2 × 10⁷) ≈ 3.1 × 10³ m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 9.5 × 10⁶, which is v².

questions.stem: Satellite A orbits a planet at radius r with period T. Satellite B orbits the same planet at radius 4r. What is the period of satellite B?
questions.explanation: For circular orbits, T² = 4π²r³/(GM), so T² ∝ r³. Multiplying r by 4 multiplies T² by 4³ = 64, so T is multiplied by √64 = 8. Assuming T is proportional to r gives 4T, and assuming T² is proportional to r gives 2T.

questions.stem: A 500 kg satellite and a 2000 kg satellite orbit Earth at the same radius. Compared with the lighter satellite, the heavier one has:
options: the same speed but a longer period
the same speed and the same period
a lower speed and a longer period
a higher speed and a shorter period
questions.explanation: The satellite’s mass cancels from GMm/r² = mv²/r, leaving v = √(GM/r), which depends only on Earth’s mass and the orbital radius. With the same speed and the same circumference, the periods are also the same.

questions.stem: Astronauts on a space station about 400 km above Earth feel weightless mainly because:
options: they and the station are in free fall together, so the normal force on them is zero
the gravitational field strength at that altitude is very nearly zero
an outward centrifugal force exactly balances their weight in orbit
the centripetal force on them balances their weight, so the net force is zero
questions.explanation: At 400 km, g is still close to 90% of its surface value. The astronauts and station fall towards Earth together with the same acceleration, so nothing pushes on the astronauts and they feel no normal force. The net force on them is not zero: gravity is the unbalanced centripetal force.

questions.stem: One side of a 50-turn rectangular coil is 0.040 m long and lies perpendicular to a 0.10 T magnetic field. The coil carries 2.0 A. What is the size of the force on that side?
questions.explanation: F = nIlB = 50 × 2.0 × 0.040 × 0.10 = 0.40 N. Leaving out the number of turns gives 8.0 × 10⁻³ N. Leaving out the field strength gives 4.0, which is not a force at all.

questions.stem: A horizontal wire carries a current towards the east through a uniform magnetic field directed north. What is the direction of the force on the wire?
questions.explanation: The force is perpendicular to both the current and the field. Using the right-hand rule with the current east and the field north, the force is vertically upward. The force can never be along the field, so north is ruled out.

questions.stem: In a simple DC motor, what does the split ring commutator do?
options: It reverses the current in the coil every half turn
It reverses the external magnetic field every half turn
It turns the DC supply into AC in the external circuit
It keeps the coil’s current in one direction at all times
questions.explanation: The commutator swaps the coil’s connections to the brushes every half turn, reversing the current in the coil. The magnets’ field is not affected, and the current in the external circuit stays DC.

questions.stem: Why must the current in the coil of a simple DC motor reverse every half turn?
options: So the torque keeps turning the coil in the same direction
So the coil does not overheat from a constant current
So the field of the permanent magnets is kept reversing
So the forces on the coil’s sides stay parallel to the field
questions.explanation: After the coil passes the position perpendicular to the field, the forces on its sides would turn it back the other way if the current stayed the same. Reversing the current reverses those forces, so the torque keeps the coil rotating in one direction.

questions.stem: In a simple DC motor, the coil rotates in a uniform magnetic field. The torque on the coil is greatest when the plane of the coil is:
options: at any angle, as the torque is constant
questions.explanation: When the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, the forces on the sides are perpendicular to the plane, so they act at the greatest distance from the axis and give the greatest torque. When the plane is perpendicular to the field, the forces act through the axis and the torque is zero.

questions.stem: Which change would increase the torque on the coil of a simple DC motor?
options: Using a weaker external magnetic field
Using fewer loops at the same current
Winding more loops of wire on the coil
Reversing the direction of the current
questions.explanation: The force on each side of the coil is F = nIlB, so torque increases with the number of loops, the current and the field strength. Reversing the current reverses the direction of rotation but not the size of the torque.

questions.stem: In a synchrotron, such as the one in Clayton in Melbourne, which job does each field do?
options: Electric fields both speed the electrons up and bend their path
Electric fields speed the electrons up; magnetic fields bend their path
Magnetic fields speed the electrons up; electric fields bend their path
Magnetic fields both speed the electrons up and bend their path
questions.explanation: An electric field does work on a charge, W = qV, so it increases the electrons’ kinetic energy. A magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work; it only changes direction, keeping the electrons on their circular path.

questions.stem: Model electrons in a storage ring as moving at speeds well below c. If the electrons are given more speed, how must the magnetic field change to keep the radius of their path the same?
options: Decrease in proportion to their speed
Increase with the square of their speed
Stay the same, as r depends only on charge
Increase in proportion to their speed
questions.explanation: From r = mv/(qB), keeping r constant needs B to rise in proportion to v. With the field unchanged, faster electrons would follow a larger circle and hit the walls. The square of speed would appear for kinetic energy, not for this radius.
